projects.title: Ava
projects.description:
Every developer now has an AI agent that can write code. None of them can move money.

Your agent can design a yield strategy, find the best rate on Monad, and explain exactly which contract to call. Then it stops, because there is a wall between what an agent knows and what an agent can do. Ava removes that wall. 

Live Demo at - https://x.com/kamalbuilds/status/2084503310061703581

WHAT ?

Ava is the execution layer your coding agent plugs into. One command connects Claude Code, Codex, or any MCP client:

claude mcp add ava --transport http "https://ava-v4-api.fly.dev/mcp?toolsets=discovery,advisory"

Your agent gains three things: a wallet it provisions itself through Turnkey, a policy engine that gates every action before it happens, and every major protocol on Monad behind a single natural-language interface.

Ask for "earn 250 USDC on monad" and Ava recognises the intent, checks it against policy, routes it to Aave v3 on chain 143, builds the calldata, signs it with the agent's own wallet, and settles it on Monad mainnet. Ask for a chain with no verified venue and it refuses rather than inventing a market, because a plausible-looking wrong address is worse than no answer.

PROOF, NOT CLAIMS

Ava signed and settled on Monad mainnet:

https://monadscan.com/tx/0x50940c9510bef0cb595ecaf2b40d57d4cfa04227b6568ded4ea0541abd8715cf

Block 92954146, status success, 1 USDC supplied into Aave v3. 

The wallet for claude ai agent at 0x648530A71280B27558B4F2cAC31dcceDcbACe77c was provisioned by Ava through Turnkey and signed both the approve and the supply. The filled amount is decoded from the confirmed on-chain Supply event rather than echoed back from the request, so a number Ava reports is a number the chain agreed to.

10 protocols live on Monad Mainnet with ONE INTENT LAYER

Aave v3, Uniswap v3 and v4 (the Monad-native central limit order book), Euler v2, Morpho, Curvance, Pendle, Perpl, and liquid staking through shMON, gMON and aprMON.

Every address was taken from a first-party source and then read back from live Monad RPC before it was written into config. Each integration is exercised end to end against real Monad state before shipping, so the calldata in the demo is the same calldata the tests run.

WHY MONAD

Sub-second blocks and fractions of a cent are what make an agent loop viable. Monitor, decide, execute, repeat. That loop is uneconomic on a chain where every action costs a dollar and takes a minute. Monad is the first EVM chain where an autonomous agent can afford to actually act, continuously, rather than propose once and wait for a human.

TRY IT

Demo: https://monad.getava.xyz

Everything in there is checkable: the tx resolves on monadscan, the MCP command connects, the demo page loads, the repo is public.

Two deliberate choices. I named the wallet address so a judge can look up its history and see Ava's own transactions rather than taking the claim on trust. And I kept the fail-closed behaviour in, because "it refuses" is a stronger signal of engineering maturity than another feature bullet, especially to judges who have seen a lot of demos that confidently do the wrong thing.

projects.title: SKIN
projects.description:
Copy-trading is heads-I-win-tails-you-lose. A trader publishes a strategy, you follow with your money — if he wins he takes a fee, if he loses he loses nothing. It wasn't his capital at risk, so his optimal play is to maximise variance with yours.
SKIN fixes the payoff, not the marketing. The vault is sliced into three tranches — senior, junior, and equity — and losses fill from the bottom up. The leader sits in equity, so his own money absorbs every loss first. He can't withdraw below a 10% floor while a position is open, can't leverage past 5x, can't whipsaw followers (recoveries repay write-downs before any coupon or residual), and can't curate his record — every closed position, win or lose, is booked on-chain by the same transaction that settles the P&L.
Yields aren't hardcoded either. Each tranche's coupon is priced off how much protection genuinely sits beneath it, so as the leader drains, follower yields climb automatically watch it happen live on the app.

None of this works on a slow chain. A tranche is a promise about the order losses land in, and that promise only holds if you can mark to market faster than losses arrive. On a 12-second chain the leader has a window every block to exit at a stale price before his losses register. On Monad, marks land every 400ms — the same cadence Pyth publishes MON/USD — so that window shrinks to nothing. This isn't tranches with better UX; it's tranches that are actually enforceable.
Anyone can launch a vault through the factory, which refuses leaders unwilling to stake themselves. Followers sign in with a passkey — no seed phrase.
Both contracts are verified on Monad testnet, 39 tests including two fuzzed invariants, and the full cascade has fired on a real MON price move.

projects.title: Orbital
projects.description:
a spherical AMM which supports multi-token pools like Curve and provides the concentrated liquidity of Uniswap v3, both at once, which no pool in production does today. It is an implementation of Orbital, the AMM paper published by Paradigm, shipped as a Uniswap v4 hook and deployed on Monad testnet. Four stablecoins share one reserve book inside the hook, which prices them on a sphere rather than on Uniswap's constant-product curve, so a whole basket of dollars trades against a single deep pool.


PROBLEM 

Stablecoins all target the same dollar, but every AMM in production makes you choose between holding many of them and holding them deeply.

Curve takes the first path. It keeps a whole basket in one pool, but lays liquidity flat along the entire curve, so most of the capital ends up parked at prices a dollar will never reach while the peg, where stablecoins actually trade, stays thin. In practice that works out to roughly one to two times the capital efficiency of a flat curve.

Uniswap v3 takes the second path. It concentrates liquidity exactly where trades land, which is far more efficient, and then caps the pool at two tokens. Because every pool is a pair, a four-coin basket has to fragment into six separate markets, each shallower than the last, and liquidity sitting in USDC/USDT does nothing for someone trading USDC against FRAX.

The deeper problem is what happens when a coin fails. A flat stable pool goes on quoting a broken asset near a dollar long after the market has repriced it, so arbitrage sells the failing coin in and takes the healthy ones out until the LPs are left holding almost nothing else. That is the tail impermanent loss which wiped out stable LPs when USDC fell to eighty-eight cents in March 2023, and it is a direct consequence of the pool having no way to express a limit on what it is willing to hold.


SOLUTION

All three problems come from the same place, which is the shape of the curve, so Orbital changes the shape. Where Uniswap prices two tokens on a hyperbola, x times y equals k, Orbital prices N tokens on a sphere, where the squared distance from the reserve vector to the centre equals the radius squared.

The sphere. The pool's reserve vector is a point on an N-dimensional sphere of radius r centred at (r, ..., r). The peg is the equal-price point, where every coin trades exactly one to one. The curve is almost flat there and only begins to bend as the basket drifts away from the peg, which is precisely the behaviour you want from a stablecoin venue.

The ticks. Each LP cuts that sphere with a plane of their own, set at whatever depeg they are willing to hold, for example "provide liquidity only while this coin stays above ninety-five cents". Capital then packs into the narrow band around the peg instead of being smeared across prices that never occur, and because the curve below the bound is removed, a modest real deposit behaves like a far larger reserve. This is the same virtual-liquidity idea behind Uniswap v3, generalised from a pair to an N-sphere.

The torus. Every one of those planes stacks into a single torus that the pool tracks with just two running sums, the sum of the reserves and the sum of their squares, so a swap costs the same whether the basket holds four coins or forty.

That same plane is also what makes a depeg survivable. When a coin crosses the bound an LP chose, their tick moves to the boundary and stops quoting, so the pool stops absorbing the failing asset while every healthy coin keeps trading one to one against the others. Nothing has to be voted on and nothing has to be paused. The isolation is a property of where the plane sits on the sphere, so it happens the moment the bound is crossed, and each LP's downside is capped at the limit they set when they deposited.


WHAT IT PROVIDES

- Multi-token pools, not pairs. A single pool prices a whole basket off one sphere. Four stablecoins would normally need six separate markets; here the six pairs are only views onto one shared reserve vector, and listing a fifth coin adds a dimension rather than four more markets.

- No liquidity fragmentation. Because the pairs share one book, a USDC/FRAX trade draws on exactly the same liquidity as USDC/USDT. One deep pool instead of six thin ones.

- Concentrated liquidity in N dimensions. Each LP sets their own depeg bound, so capital sits in the narrow band around the peg where stablecoins actually trade instead of being spread across prices that never happen.

- Higher capital efficiency. A tick removes the curve below its bound, so a small real deposit behaves like a much larger reserve. Measured at about 154 times a flat curve on the live deployment.

- Lower slippage. A hundred-thousand-dollar swap moves the price 0.0145 percent, of which the 1 basis point pool fee is most of it, leaving under half a basis point of true price impact.

- Automatic depeg isolation. When a coin breaks peg its tick exits to the boundary and the rest keep trading one to one, so a single broken coin cannot drain the LPs who supplied the others. Loss is bounded by the plane the LP chose.

- Constant-time swaps. Interior and boundary ticks consolidate into one torus invariant, so a swap stays O(1) no matter how many assets or ticks the pool holds.

- Built on v4, not beside it. The hook supplies only the curve. Custody, flash accounting and the unlock and settle flow are all v4's, so any router or aggregator that already speaks v4 can trade against it. Tokens never leave the PoolManager and the hook settles entirely in ERC-6909 claim tokens.


MEASURED ON THE LIVE DEPLOYMENT

Quoted through the V4Quoter against the deployed hook, on roughly 20 million dollars of capital, a 10,000 dollar swap costs 0.0104 percent, a 100,000 dollar swap costs 0.0145 percent, and a 1,000,000 dollar swap costs 0.0545 percent. The 0.0100 percent floor is the 1 basis point pool fee, so pure price impact on a hundred-thousand-dollar swap is 0.0045 percent. Capital efficiency at the peg measures about 154 times a flat curve. 121 tests pass, including a solvency invariant.

projects.title: ATRUM-Private Prediction Markets on Monad
projects.description:
Atrum: private prediction market on Monad, atrum.fun.

Users bet YES or NO on a single real-world event. Individual bets, identities and balances stay hidden from everyone, including the operator, while odds stay public and settlement is publicly verifiable. Deposits are public (funding the pool from a wallet, by design), but betting, redeeming, and withdrawing run through proof-gated relayed actions so a user's address never appears next to their own bet.

Under the hood: Groth16 zero-knowledge proofs over BN254 (circom, snarkjs) prove a bet is valid without revealing which deposit funded it. Bet amounts use exponential ElGamal encryption on BabyJubJub, additively homomorphic so pool totals can be tallied without decrypting individual bets, hence a parimutuel design rather than an order book or AMM. Poseidon hashing and a depth-20 Merkle tree (with subtree grafting for gas) track note commitments, a mapping-based nullifier set stops double-spends. A TypeScript/viem sequencer batches commitments and relays proof-gated actions, keeping liveness and ordering trust separate from custody of funds.

Front end is Next.js, driving the full deposit to bet to settle to redeem to withdraw lifecycle against live Monad testnet, plus a separate scroll-driven 3D landing page (React Three Fiber, GSAP, Motion, Lenis) explaining the six-act story of what it is and why to join.

Paylox lets AI agents actually use money without giving them unlimited control over your wallet.

You can give an agent like Claude or ChatGPT a wallet on Monad and ask it to do things like send MON, pay someone, or deploy a contract, directly from the chat you already use.

The problem is that AI agents can make mistakes. And when money is involved, one wrong address or wrong amount is enough to cause a real problem.

So with Paylox, you set the rules first.

For example, you can say that an agent is allowed to pay a specific vendor, only to a specific address, and only up to a certain amount.

Whenever the agent tries to make a payment, Paylox checks it against those rules before any money moves.

If everything matches, the payment goes through on Monad.

If something looks wrong, Paylox blocks it and tells you what failed. Nothing leaves the wallet.

The rules are enforced through an on-chain escrow contract, so a blocked payment is actually blocked, not just shown as a warning that the agent can ignore.

Paylox also connects through MCP, so you can use it with agents like Claude without installing another SDK or building a completely new agent around it.

The idea is pretty simple: agents should be able to spend money and do useful things onchain, but they should only be able to do what you actually gave them permission to do.

projects.title: Synod
projects.description:
Synod is an on-chain circuit breaker for autonomous trading agents. AI agents are increasingly executing trades with real capital and no independent check — one model, one decision, no second opinion. Synod fixes that by requiring a reputation-weighted quorum of independent agents to approve a trade before it executes.

Here's how it works: agents commit a hashed vote first and only reveal it after the window closes, preventing vote-copying or front-running. Votes are weighted by each agent's on-chain reputation, which moves via an exponential moving average based on whether their past votes matched the resolved outcome. Funds sit in a reentrancy-protected escrow the entire time and only release automatically once weighted consensus crosses the quorum threshold. An emergency pause exists, but it's gated behind a 60-second Timelock rather than a single admin key.

What makes it special is that the agents aren't simulated opinions dressed up for a demo. Alongside a swarm proving the system holds up under real parallel load, Synod runs a five-agent AI Council with genuine reasoning from Sarvam AI and Groq's Llama 3.3 70B, independently verified via raw API response logs and a poisoned-API-key fallback test. Every vote, every rationale, and every reputation change is permanently on-chain. And it's built on Monad specifically because the check can't be slower than the trade it's protecting: ten agents commit and reveal in parallel, resolving in consecutive blocks in well under a second, visible live in the demo rather than claimed in a slide.

projects.title: Monad Auctions
projects.description:
A token launchpad where the launch price is discovered by an auction instead of guessed by the deployer — and where placing a bid costs nothing, requires no gas, and writes nothing on-chain unless you win.

Supply is released into the market over rounds on a CCA schedule. Bidders submit a demand curve — a ladder of (price, quantity), each one a gasless x402 upto authorization signed in their wallet. Each round the engine finds the single uniform clearing price that fills the remaining supply against the order book, fills everyone above it, splits the marginal tick pro-rata, and settles. Everyone who fills pays the same price, which is below what they bid. Everyone who doesn't fill pays nothing — their USDC balance after losing is byte-identical to before.

Verified end-to-end on Monad testnet: 13 rounds, 219 bids, 54 transactions, 120/120 units cleared, 1.455 USDC to the seller, 0.612 USDC of buyer surplus, rounds completing in ~0.6s wall clock.

The core insight: upto is a sealed bid
x402's upto scheme is documented as a metering primitive — authorize a maximum, charge actual usage. Read it as an auction primitive and a uniform-price auction falls out for free:

upto mechanic	Auction meaning
Signed maximum	the bid
Settle ≤ max	the clearing price — the winner is charged less than they bid
$0 settlement, no tx	losing costs nothing
Permit2 witness binds to	proceeds cannot be redirected
Permit2 nonce	a bid cannot be replayed
Facilitator pays gas	bidding is gasless
This isn't a mechanism layered on top of x402. Charging below the signed ceiling is upto's settlement rule; a uniform-price auction is just what you get when you use it on a whole order book at once. And because CCA already quantises bids to price ticks, one authorization per tick gives you a cryptographically-capped signed demand curve.

The cap is enforced by math, not promises: the x402 Permit2 proxy reverts with AmountExceedsPermitted if the operator tries to charge above your signed ceiling. You do not have to trust the launchpad not to overcharge you — it can't.

Why this is a fairer launch than the alternatives
vs. pump.fun / bonding curves
A bonding curve fixes price as a function of how much supply has already sold. The price schedule is written before anyone has expressed demand, so nothing about it is discovery — it's a posted price list with a queue attached.

The consequence is that the first buyer always gets the lowest price, regardless of how much they actually value the token. That is a mechanical reward for latency, not for conviction. Sniper bots in the first blocks buy the bottom of the curve and sell to the humans arriving behind them; the value that should have gone to the project or to genuine buyers is captured by whoever had the fastest infrastructure. Being 300ms earlier is worth more than believing in the project.

In the CCA, time within a round is worth exactly nothing. Bid at the start of the round or a millisecond before it closes: you get the same uniform price. There is no ordering advantage to buy, so there is no gas war, no sniping, and no MEV extraction around the launch. What you're rewarded for is being early across rounds and honest about your price — which is the behaviour you actually want to encourage.

vs. seeding a Uniswap pool at some ratio
Adding liquidity at a chosen ratio means the deployer picks the launch price by hand, before demand is known. There are only two ways that goes:

Priced too low → the pool is instantly arbitraged. The first transaction in the pool buys the mispricing, and the surplus flows to a searcher and the validator who ordered them first. The project raised less than it could have and the gap became someone else's MEV.
Priced too high → nothing fills, the chart is red from block one, and the launch is dead on arrival.
The launchpad's entire first-block dynamic becomes a priority-gas auction for the right to buy underpriced tokens — an auction is happening either way, it's just an auction whose proceeds go to searchers instead of to the seller.

The CCA runs that auction explicitly, and pays the proceeds to the right party.

Measured against the actual spread of prices a seller might have guessed:

price the seller guesses	units sold	revenue
0.005	120	0.600
0.013	120	1.560
0.016	102	1.632 ← best, only visible in hindsight
0.018	70	1.260
0.020	36	0.720
auction	120	1.455
The auction beats the average guess by 1.26×, the median by 1.15×, and the worst by 2.42×. It gives up 11% against the best guess — against an oracle that does not exist, and that no deployer has access to at launch time. The trade isn't "auction vs. the best fixed price"; it's "the auction removes the guess."

The fairness properties, stated plainly
One price for everyone in a round. No buyer pays more than another for the same block of supply. Whales and retail clear at the same number.
Winners pay less than they bid. 0.612 USDC of measured surplus went to buyers, not to the seller and not to a sniper. Bidding your true maximum doesn't mean paying it.
Losing is free. No gas, no fee, no state written. This is what makes honest bidding safe — there is no cost to revealing what you'd actually pay, so the demand curve the price is computed from is a real one.
No latency advantage, therefore no MEV. Nothing about ordering within a round changes an outcome, so there is nothing to bid gas for.
Early conviction is rewarded, not early reflexes. Because supply is released over rounds and unfilled demand rolls over, the clearing price ratchets up as supply is consumed (0.011 → 0.013 in the real run). Early rounds clear cheaper, so early bidders realize a genuine discount — measurable as the gap between blended market cap (what the book actually realized) and spot market cap (what the marginal buyer is underwriting now).
The whole thing is checkable. Every round publishes the full bid set with signatures, hash-chained to the previous round. verify_proof.py re-derives every clearing price from scratch, verifies all 219 signatures — winners and losers — and confirms on-chain that no winner was charged above the cleared price. A fabricated losing bid injected to lift the price is caught twice over.
Why Monad, specifically
Bids are free, so cost scales with winners — not with bidders. 219 bids produced 54 transactions. In Uniswap's own on-chain CCA, placing a bid is a transaction; here a bid is an off-chain signature and only fills ever touch the chain. An auction with hundreds of participants costs the price of a few dozen transfers. That is what makes a genuinely open launch — anyone can bid, and the cost of letting them doesn't scale with how many show up.

Continuous actually means continuous. CCA is designed for continuous time. On Ethereum it can only clear every 12s — continuous in name only. Monad's ~0.3s blocks clear it ~40× finer, and full rounds settle in ~0.6s wall clock, with multiple settlements landing in the same block. A launch that reprices 40× more often tracks demand instead of lagging it, and the gap a sniper could exploit shrinks toward zero.

Fills fan out. A bidder filled across five price ticks means five transfers. That's prohibitive on L1 and noise on Monad — which is what allows a real demand curve rather than a single flat order.

Stablecoin denomination. Settlement is in USDC via x402, so price discovery happens in dollars. "This round cleared at 0.013 USDC" is a number that means something to a buyer and to the treasury — the launch price isn't entangled with the volatility of the gas token, and the seller's proceeds don't need hedging.

Gasless for the bidder. The facilitator pays gas for settlement. The only transaction a participant ever signs is a one-time Permit2 approve. Bidding — the part everyone does, repeatedly, across every round — is a signature.

projects.title: Umbra — Universal Shielded Wallet
projects.description:
Privacy for any ERC-20, on Monad speed

Umbra is a universal shielded wallet for Monad — a privacy layer that works with any standard ERC-20 token, not just a single allowlisted asset. Users deposit tokens into a shared shielded pool, then transact privately inside it: sending value without revealing the asset, amount, sender, or recipient on-chain. Withdrawals return funds to a public address, either self-submitted or gaslessly through a relayer.
Under the hood, Umbra runs on a Noir zero-knowledge circuit (two inputs, two outputs per transaction) verified by an immutable Solidity contract with no owner, no pause, and no privileged withdrawal path — the pool custodies funds permissionlessly. A depth-32 Merkle tree and Poseidon2 commitments track shielded state; nullifiers prevent double-spending.
Monad is what makes this practical rather than theoretical: sub-second finality means a shielded transfer confirms while the user is still watching, closing the UX gap that makes privacy tech feel unusable on slower EVM chains. Built end-to-end in one day at Monad Blitz Toronto: circuit, contracts, and a full deposit → transfer → withdraw wallet frontend.

Whether it's a tutor session, babysitter, parking spot, coworking desk, or AI service, TickPay makes every second count. Start when you begin. Stop when you’re done. The unused balance instantly returns to you.
Built on Monad’s high-performance infrastructure, TickPay brings fairness, transparency, and programmable payments to everyday transactions.
No overpaying. No forgotten subscriptions. No wasted time. Just pay-per-use, powered by the blockchain.

projects.title: MONAD | GATE
projects.description:
MONAD | Gate is a permission-and-proof layer for autonomous agents on Monad. An agent wallet is bound on-chain to a human principal who remains liable, the principal sets a narrow action-and-spend policy, and the contract itself refuses anything outside it — the front-end cannot approve what the chain rejects. Every allowed action emits an ActionAttested event tying agent, principal, action, amount and an off-chain result hash together, so each permitted action leaves a receipt anyone can verify.

Live on Monad testnet (chain 10143). Contract: 0x7feaAb7D9634E6F614e28a42E800E6a7237d37C2. Agent registration, policy, and a real attestation are already on-chain: a 100-unit request against a 10-unit cap reverts with SpendCapExceeded(100, 10), while a 5-unit request succeeds and attests. Authorization is enforced on-chain too — policy changes by a non-principal revert with NotPrincipal, and replayed result hashes revert with ResultAlreadyAttested.

projects.title: LastUnit
projects.description:
LastUnit — verified-presence flash drops on Monad

Live: https://last-unit.burnedcore.com
Contract (Monad testnet, chain 10143): 0x0675a899e19Fe66D99dAD97e76763A49B8aa3A74
https://testnet.monadvision.com/address/0x0675a899e19Fe66D99dAD97e76763A49B8aa3A74

A limited product drop that can only be claimed by people physically standing in the store.

A display in the store shows a QR code that is re-signed and re-issued every second, carrying a beacon signature and the current block height. Scanning it opens a page that generates a key in the browser, signs the challenge, and submits a claim through a relayer pool — no wallet, no tokens, no install. The contract rejects any challenge older than its freshness window, measured in blocks.

Someone can screenshot the QR and forward it to a friend outside the store. That claim is also valid — it just arrives a few seconds later, because a relay carries extra hops. At ~300ms blocks that's roughly 20 blocks of lag. When two units are left and ordering is settled by consensus, a few seconds is the difference between getting one and getting nothing. We don't block the cheat. We make it lose.

Claims mint a soulbound receipt. At the counter, the buyer's phone shows a 6-digit code backed by an owner signature that re-signs every second against the current block; the cashier enters it, the contract verifies ownership and freshness, burns the token, and signals the staff to hand over the goods. The gap between claimed and redeemed is a no-show metric retail can't currently measure.

Why Monad: both properties are chain-enforced, not vendor-promised, and both need blocks shorter than a human action. Freshness of 50 blocks is 15 seconds here and 10 minutes on Ethereum — same contract, same constant, one of them useless. And ordering only exists if block time is finer than the spread between arrivals; at 12s two people seconds apart land in one block and the builder decides, not reality. Claims are submitted from a pool of independent senders so no single nonce sequence — including ours — dictates the order.

Live on Monad testnet. Solidity/Foundry contract with EIP-191 dual-signature verification, Next.js app with three surfaces (store display, claim page, presenter wall), server-side beacon and relayer, in-memory indexer over Claimed/Redeemed events streamed to the UI. Measured on the day: ~300ms blocks, 400ms ordering resolution, receipts in 150–500ms via eth_sendRawTransactionSync.
Deliberate shortcuts: centralized relayer, one key per device rather than real identity, testnet only. Sybil resistance is the cashier who sees a face — retail solved "one per customer" a century ago, and we don't try to replace that with cryptography.

A protocol puts up its contract with a USDC reward pool and a hidden rule that must never break. Then a swarm of autonomous AI hacker-agents goes to work — each one stakes its own money, writes its own exploit, and submits it. Talk is worthless; only a working hack gets paid.

It's agent-to-agent end to end: the sponsor, the auditors, the payments — all autonomous, all onchain. The result is continuous, adversarial security — instead of a one-time review, an endless line of AI auditors keeps attacking your code, and you only ever pay for exploits that actually work.

In one line: continuous, agent-driven smart-contract auditing where a bounty pays only for exploits that provably work — settled onchain in USDC on Monad.

projects.title: Castle
projects.description:
Castle is the trust layer for the AI agent economy: a system that lets an autonomous AI agent transact on-chain at Monad speed while the human owner keeps absolute, revocable control. Every owner deploys their own per-agent smart-contract wallet (`CastleWallet`) through an on-chain factory, funds it with MON, and then attaches one or more **active session keys** to it, each representing a live AI session (a ChatGPT run, a Claude worker, a Cursor loop) with its own bounded permissions. Instead of handing an agent a raw private key (a total-loss risk on any prompt injection or leak) or hiding it behind a custodial API (which defeats the point of a permissionless agent), Castle enforces the agent's rules in the wallet contract itself: every active session key has a hard expiry, a rolling 24-hour daily spend cap, a single allowed target contract, and a function-selector allow-list, so any request outside the fence reverts on-chain, every time; an owner can run many sessions in parallel on one wallet (marketplace worker, payment agent, custom policy) and see each one live in the dashboard with remaining budget, IP history, and status (Active, Expired, Frozen). On top of that, an off-chain safety net simulates every write via `eth_call` before broadcast, encrypts each session's private key with AES-256-GCM, monitors IPs and repeated transaction patterns per session, and pings the owner on Telegram for Approve / Reject on high-value actions, while `freezeAgent` and batch controls let the owner revoke every active session across every wallet in one transaction and `emergencyWithdraw` sweeps the balance home in a single block. The result is a complete four-layer product (four Solidity contracts on Monad, a Next.js 16 owner console with wallet and session management, an Express REST API the agent drives with a bearer token, and a Supabase-backed monitoring stack) that takes an LLM from zero to a live, policy-bound session in about sixty seconds, turning what is today a catastrophic-loss risk into a bounded, recoverable, human-supervised workflow, and giving the emerging agent economy the on-chain primitive of trust it needs to actually move real money at machine speed.
In short: agents transact at machine speed inside a fence the blockchain enforces.

projects.description:
CrossCheck is a verification and payment layer for autonomous AI coding agents. When an AI agent is hired to fix a bug, there's currently no reliable way to know if the fix actually works — an LLM "reviewing" a diff can be fooled the same way the original agent can cheat. CrossCheck solves this with a deterministic reviewer that actually runs the test suite inside a locked-down Docker sandbox, checks for the AI-specific failure mode of gaming tests (deleting assertions, weakening checks, hardcoding outputs), and writes the verdict on-chain.
If the patch genuinely passes: the result goes to the ERC-8004 Reputation Registry tied to the worker agent's on-chain identity, and payment settles automatically via x402. If the agent cheated or the fix fails: the verdict still gets written (reputation drops, publicly visible), and payment never settles.
The core insight: trust in autonomous agents shouldn't come from another AI's opinion — it should come from a fact anchored to code that actually ran, with a small transparent rule set (not a prompt) doing the judging. This ties an agent's permanent public reputation and its payment directly to real verified outcomes, closing the trust gap that's currently the main bottleneck to letting coding agents operate autonomously.

Three core capabilities: (1) Sovereign Vault — agent memory tied to a did:monad DID, not a platform account. Operator-owned keys. Switch models, keep memory. Every memory write generates a SHA-256 fingerprint batched onto Monad via AttestationAggregator.sol. GDPR Right to Erasure is enforced on-chain via DeletionProver.sol — cryptographic tombstones that give compliance officers exportable proof of deletion. Monad's 10,000 TPS and sub-second finality make the attestation volume economically viable at ~$0.001 per attestation.

projects.title: MonadStamp
projects.description:
MonadStamp is a physical event check-in dApp built on Monad Testnet. When an attendee scans a QR code at an event, they receive a Soul-bound NFT (SBT) minted instantly to their wallet — no gas required, no centralized server, no middleman.
The core problem it solves: Existing attendance records live on platforms like Luma or Eventbrite. If the platform goes down, the data disappears. Records can be faked, deleted, or made inaccessible. There is no truly verifiable, permanent proof of attendance.
Why Monad makes it possible: When 300 people scan QR codes simultaneously at an event exit, all 300 mint transactions are processed in the same block thanks to Monad's parallel EVM and 10,000 TPS throughput. On Ethereum this would take minutes. On Polygon transactions queue up. Only Monad enables true real-time, simultaneous mass minting.
How it works:

Organizer generates an event QR code via the admin panel
Attendee scans → signs an EIP-712 message (no gas paid)
Gasless relay submits the mint transaction to Monad
Soul-bound NFT lands in the attendee's wallet in under 1 second
Live dashboard shows every mint in real time as they happen

What makes it different from POAP: POAP relies on centralized claim links and slow transaction confirmations. MonadStamp is fully on-chain, gasless for the user, transfer-locked, and composable — other smart contracts can use the SBT as an access condition.
MonadStamp is not a Luma competitor. It is a layer on top — any organizer with a Luma Plus account can plug MonadStamp in. The attendance record moves from a private server to a public, permanent, verifiable chain.

projects.title: Agent-Tale
projects.description:
Agent-Tale'in "Case Bridge" modülü, iki farklı proje veya API bağlayıcısı (connector) arasındaki verileri sorunsuz bir şekilde birbirine bağlamak, karşılaştırmak ve birleştirmek için tasarlanmış özel bir entegrasyon aracıdır. Bu özelliği özel kılan şey, çok adımlı ve yapılandırılmış mutabakat (reconciliation) motorudur.

Süreç ilk olarak, iki tarafın da birleştirilmiş JSON çıktı formatını kriptografik olarak imzalayıp onayladığı asenkron bir "Consensus" (Mutabakat) mekanizmasıyla başlar. Eşleşme sağlandıktan sonra motor analitik durumları (Cases) çalıştırır: "Case 1" arka planda bir Proje Fark Matrisi (Project Diff Matrix) oluşturur ve özellikleri Ortak (Common), Uyumlu (Compatible), Uyumsuz (Incompatible) ve Farklı (Different) değişkenler olarak dinamik bir 2x2 ızgarada kategorize eder. "Case 2" ise bir Uç Nokta Birleştirme (Endpoint Merge) işlemi yürüterek, farklı kaynaklardan gelen API rotalarını otomatik olarak tek bir tabloda birleştirir ve bu süreçte otonom ToolSet'ler oluşturmak için "MCP (Model Context Protocol) Fırsatlarını" tespit eder. projects.title: soz
projects.description:
Soz is a collective pledge vault that truly leverages Monad's parallel execution capabilities. Users lock their PLEDGE tokens for a set period—acting not as a vehicle for speculation, but as a self-custody discipline and savings tool.

The key engineering decision: each user writes only to their *own* storage slot (`balances[msg.sender]`, `locked[msg.sender]`). There is no shared pool, global counter, or pooled custody. Consequently, when hundreds of people lock simultaneously, there is zero state contention, allowing Monad to process all transactions in parallel within a single block. Aggregate statistics are calculated via off-chain event indexing rather than on-chain counters.

Why Monad? A "naive" design (where everyone writes to a single pool balance) would cause contention on that single slot, forcing Monad to serialize the transactions—thereby killing parallelism. By partitioning state on a per-user basis, Söz becomes a perfect showcase for Monad's parallel engine: 150 transactions, 0 shared slots, 1 block.

Demo: Everyone in the room signs a lock transaction via QR code simultaneously; a 150-cell grid on the screen turns green in parallel within seconds, with no gas spikes. A side-by-side comparison of "Naive (shared pool) vs. Söz (partitioned state)" visually demonstrates this difference.

Stack: Solidity (Foundry) + Next.js/viem, Monad Testnet (chainId 10143).
Team: Seyit (frontend/product/demo) + Bekir (smart contracts).
